finding.claim: The DELETE handler calls the async authorize() without await. A forbidden user's denial becomes an unhandled promise rejection and the deletion proceeds, so any authenticated user can delete any report.
finding.source: Any authenticated user sending DELETE /reports/:id with an arbitrary id (req.params.id).

trace.note: authorize() is called without await, so the returned promise is ignored.
The 403 error is thrown inside the async function and only rejects the discarded promise.
db.reports.remove runs regardless of the authorization result.
The handler returns 204, so the attacker sees success.

finding.guards_checked: The authorize() check exists but is not awaited. The PUT handler at line 27 awaits it correctly, which confirms the DELETE handler is the outlier. No other middleware enforces authorization. The global middleware only copies req.session.user. Express 4 does not catch the floating rejection, and on modern Node an unhandled rejection can also crash the process.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws on denial, but the DELETE handler at line 20 calls it without await, so the rejection is discarded. The only middleware (lines 4-7) copies the session user and does no authorization. The PUT handler at line 27 awaits it correctly.
verdict.reason: server.js:20 calls async authorize() as a bare statement, so the 403 thrown at server.js:14 only rejects an ignored promise and db.reports.remove at server.js:21 runs for any user who is authenticated and not authorized.

finding.claim: The auth middleware reads req.session.user, but no session middleware is installed, so req.session is undefined and every request throws a TypeError. If a session layer is added elsewhere, unauthenticated requests get req.user undefined, and authorize() then throws on user.id (a 500 error, not an access grant). This is a robustness and authentication-enforcement gap rather than a clear bypass.
finding.sink: req.user = req.session.user, followed by the handlers' authorize(req.user, ...)

trace.note: req.session.user is dereferenced with no session middleware and no login check.
user.id is dereferenced; this fails for a missing user.

finding.guards_checked: There is no explicit authentication check (no 401 for a missing user). The DELETE route skips authorize() effectively because of F1, so an unauthenticated request could also delete if the session layer were present and req.user were undefined. In that case the unawaited authorize() fails on user.id, but the rejection is ignored.

verdict.guard_found: none: no session middleware, no 401 check for a missing user. authorize() at server.js:9-16 throws on a missing grant but is not awaited on the DELETE route (server.js:20). The PUT route does await it (server.js:27).
verdict.reason: server.js:5 dereferences req.session.user with no session middleware (a TypeError, so Express returns 500) and no missing-user check, and server.js:10 throws on user.id when the user is undefined. The claim holds as a robustness and authentication-enforcement gap, and it fails closed today. The PUT route is safe because it awaits authorize (server.js:27). The DELETE route does not await it (server.js:20), so once a session layer is added an unauthenticated delete would go through, which is the F1 issue.
